definitions.explanation: A word of native Japanese origin, as opposed to words borrowed from Chinese (漢語) or other languages (外来語). Also called 大和言葉 (yamato kotoba).

examples.japanese: 「{山|やま}」や「{川|かわ}」は{和語|わご}だ。
{和語|わご}は{漢語|かんご}に{比|くら}べて{柔|やわ}らかい{響|ひび}きがある。
examples.english: Native Japanese words have a softer sound compared to Sino-Japanese words.

examples.japanese: {日本語|にほんご}の{語彙|ごい}は{和語|わご}、{漢語|かんご}、{外来語|がいらいご}の{三|みっ}つに{大|おお}きく{分|わ}けられ、それぞれが{異|こと}なる{特徴|とくちょう}を{持|も}っている。
examples.english: Japanese vocabulary is broadly divided into three categories — native words, Sino-Japanese words, and loanwords — each with distinct characteristics.

notes:
USAGE:
A linguistic term used when discussing the origins and layers of Japanese vocabulary. Japanese vocabulary is traditionally classified into three categories: {和語|わご} (native Japanese), {漢語|かんご} (Sino-Japanese, borrowed from Chinese), and {外来語|がいらいご} (loanwords from other languages). {和語|わご} is also called {大和言葉|やまとことば}.

KEY CHARACTERISTICS:
{和語|わご} tends to sound softer and more emotional than {漢語|かんご}. Many basic, everyday words are {和語|わご}: {食|た}べる (to eat), {歩|ある}く (to walk), {美|うつく}しい (beautiful). Kanji used for {和語|わご} are read with {訓読|くんよ}み (native readings).

COMMON COLLOCATIONS:
- {和語|わご}の{読|よ}み: native Japanese reading
- {和語|わご}と{漢語|かんご}: native and Sino-Japanese words
- {大和言葉|やまとことば}: yamato kotoba (synonym)
